chapters.title: The first sea crossings
chapters.stat: Sea level 120 m lower at the glacial maximum
chapters.text:
Anatomically modern humans reached Sahul — Australia and New Guinea, joined as one landmass at lower sea level — by about 65,000 years ago. Reaching it required crossing Wallacea, a chain of islands separated by straits that were never dry land at any point in the glacial cycle, because the sea floor between them is too deep. Even at the lowest stand, the shortest route still demanded at least one passage of 70–90 km out of sight of land, toward a destination that could not be seen from the departure beach.

No vessel survives, and none is likely to: the craft would have been organic, and the shorelines they left from are now under 100 m of water. The evidence is the arrival itself, and it is indirect in a second way — the dating is contested. Optically stimulated luminescence at Madjedbebe in northern Australia gives 65,000 ± 6,000 years (Clarkson and colleagues, 2017); Allen and O'Connell have argued from the wider set of sites for something closer to 50,000.

What the record does constrain is the kind of craft. Experimental crossings led by Yousuke Kaifu between 2016 and 2019, replicating the passage from Taiwan to the Ryukyu Islands with period materials, found that bamboo rafts made under a knot and could not hold against the 1–2 knot Kuroshio; a 7.6 m cedar dugout, paddled, covered 225 km of open water in 45 hours. If the Pleistocene sea craft was anything, it was closer to a dugout than to a raft.

There were no states, no ports and no shipwrights in this period. The societies making these crossings were mobile foraging populations, and the capability spread with them rather than being invented in one place: obsidian from Kozushima, an island 50 km off the Japanese coast, appears on Honshu from about 38,000 years ago, which means not a single crossing but repeated, deliberate return voyages for a specific material. In the Mediterranean, obsidian from Melos reaches the mainland cave of Franchthi by about 11,000 years ago on the same logic.
chapters.lede: With sea level about 70 m lower, people cross 70–90 km of open water to land that is not visible from the shore they leave.
chapters.cite: Clarkson et al., *Nature* (2017); Kealy, Louys & O'Connor (2018); Spratt & Lisiecki sea-level stack (2016).

chapters.title: Reed, plank and the earliest sea trade
chapters.text:
Bronze needs copper and tin, the two ores occur in different places, and in the Bronze Age Mediterranean the connection between them was made by sea. The wreck excavated off Uluburun in southern Turkey, dated to about 1320 BC, was a hull roughly 15 m long carrying 354 oxhide copper ingots — about ten tonnes — together with about a tonne of tin: close to the 10:1 ratio the alloy requires. Her cargo came from at least seven cultures, including Cypriot copper, Canaanite jars, Egyptian gold, Baltic amber and Mycenaean pottery.

Egyptian shipwrights were building at monumental scale considerably earlier. The vessel buried beside the Great Pyramid about 2566 BC and reassembled in the twentieth century is 43.6 m long and consists of 1,224 pieces of Lebanese cedar joined with unpegged mortise-and-tenon and lashed with grass rope. It has no keel and no frames — the hull is a shell, and its shape is held by the joinery of the planking itself, a method that remained standard in the Mediterranean for two thousand years.

The societies driving this were coastal states with something to move and the administration to finance it. Egypt imported cedar from Byblos on the Levantine coast in quantity, and sent expeditions down the Red Sea to Punt, the best documented being Hatshepsut's about 1470 BC. Minoan Crete has been described since Arthur Evans as a thalassocracy, though the extent of its naval control is debated; Mycenaean Greece, Cyprus as the principal copper source, Ugarit and the Hittite empire all appear in the same trade. In the Persian Gulf, Mesopotamian cities traded through Dilmun with the Indus valley: Indus weights and seals are found in Mesopotamia, and Mesopotamian goods in Indus ports.

The techniques were not confined to the Mediterranean. The Ferriby boats from the Humber estuary, about 2000 BC, are sewn plank craft — planks stitched edge to edge with yew withies — built with no metal fastenings at all.
chapters.lede: Bronze Age Mediterranean trade moves metal by sea, in hulls joined by mortise-and-tenon and sewn with grass cordage.
chapters.cite: Bass & Pulak, Institute of Nautical Archaeology; Khufu ship, Grand Egyptian Museum.

chapters.title: Oared fleets and the monsoon passage
chapters.text:
Two seas were worked on incompatible principles during the same centuries, and the difference was the wind. The Mediterranean is small, largely enclosed, and has no reliable seasonal wind system, so its warships were driven by oars: a galley can go where it chooses regardless of the wind, and never has far to go. The Indian Ocean has the monsoon, which reverses twice a year, and that single fact fixed its sailing calendar, its ship types and the location of its ports.

The Athenian trireme carried about 170 oarsmen in three banks and was a state instrument as much as a warship: the fleet that fought at Salamis in 480 BC was funded from the silver of Laurion, and rowing it gave the poorest citizens a claim on the constitution. Phoenician cities — Tyre, Sidon and Byblos — ran the opposite model, trading and planting colonies as far as Iberia, of which Carthage, founded by tradition in 814 BC, became the most powerful. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC and inherited the sea, then used it for bulk: the Alexandria-to-Rome grain fleet included ships of well over a thousand tonnes burden, and Portus was dug specifically to receive them.

In the Indian Ocean the monsoon made direct open-water passages possible instead of coasting. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a merchant's handbook of about AD 50, lists ports and cargoes from Egypt down the African coast and across to India with prices attached; Strabo reports something like 120 ships a year sailing from Myos Hormos on the Red Sea. Roman coin hoards in southern India and Tamil references to Yavana traders record the other end of the same route.

Meanwhile the Austronesian expansion continued across the Pacific with no connection to either system: the Lapita cultural complex spreads through Melanesia and into western Polynesia between about 1500 and 900 BC, carried by double-hulled sailing canoes into an ocean with no coastline to follow.
chapters.lede: Two seas worked on different principles: oared warships in the Mediterranean, and an Indian Ocean wind that reverses twice a year.
chapters.cite: Casson, *Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World*; *Periplus Maris Erythraei*.

chapters.title: Longships, junks and Pacific settlement
chapters.stat: Skuldelev 2: 30 m, 60 oars, built in Dublin in 1042
chapters.text:
This period has no single centre, and any account that places one in Europe is wrong on the dates. Four maritime traditions were operating at once, each solving different problems.

Norse shipwrights built clinker hulls light enough to be beached and rowed and seaworthy enough for the North Atlantic. Iceland was settled from about 870, Greenland from 985, and the Norse-built site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland has now been dated by the 993 solar storm signal in its worked wood to precisely 1021 — the first confirmed European presence in the Americas, and a small one that did not last.

Song and Yuan China had, by any technical measure, the most advanced ships afloat: watertight bulkheads dividing the hull so that one breach did not sink it, the sternpost rudder, and the magnetic compass in navigational use, described by Zhu Yu in 1119. Quanzhou and Guangzhou were among the largest ports in the world, and maritime customs revenue was a significant part of the Song state's income. The programme culminated after 1400 in Zheng He's seven voyages, 1405–1433, which reached the Persian Gulf and the East African coast before being discontinued.

The Indian Ocean was worked largely by sewn hulls carrying settee or lateen rig, with no iron in the fastenings. The Belitung wreck of about AD 830 — an Arabian-built ship lost off Indonesia with some 60,000 pieces of Chinese ceramics aboard — is a single object recording the whole route. Srivijaya controlled the straits; the Chola dynasty mounted a naval expedition against it in 1025.

And Austronesian navigators completed the settlement of the Pacific in this period, reaching Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa around 1200–1300, which are the last significant habitable landmasses on earth to be reached by people. In Europe, Venice and Genoa were building the institutions — the Arsenal, marine insurance, the commenda contract — that the following period would use.
chapters.lede: No single centre. Norse ships reach North America, Chinese hulls carry watertight bulkheads and the compass, and Pacific settlement is largely complete.
chapters.cite: Viking Ship Museum Roskilde; Needham IV.3; Belitung wreck.

chapters.title: Ocean navigation, empire and the Atlantic slave trade
chapters.stat: 12.5 million people embarked on the Middle Passage
chapters.text:
Within four centuries every ocean was crossed, charted and fought over, and the states that did it built the financial machinery to pay for it as they went.

Portugal moved first and moved south. The obstacle on the African coast was that the north-easterly trades that carry a ship down it also prevent her beating home, and the solution was the volta do mar: stand far out into the Atlantic on the return, almost to the Azores, and come back on the westerlies. That manoeuvre required a hull that could work to windward, which is what the caravel provided. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape in 1488 and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Castile went west: Columbus in 1492, and the Magellan–Elcano expedition of 1519–22, of which one ship and eighteen men completed the circumnavigation. The two crowns divided the unexplored world between themselves by the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494.

The Dutch and English then industrialised the arrangement. The VOC, chartered in 1602, was the first joint-stock company with permanent capital and tradeable shares — an instrument designed because a voyage to Asia took years and could not be financed one hull at a time; the English East India Company preceded it in 1600. The Dutch fluyt, cheap to build and worked by a small crew, cut freight costs enough to make bulk carriage profitable.

The Atlantic's largest cargo by consequence was people. An estimated 12.5 million Africans were embarked and about 10.7 million landed in the Americas across the whole trade. This was not incidental to the shipping: the between-decks of a slaver was a designed space, drawn by naval architects and optimised for a quantity of human beings per ton of burden.

Navigation lagged behind the voyaging. Latitude was straightforward; longitude was not, and was only settled when John Harrison's H4 was tested in 1761–62 and Cook demonstrated a working chronometer method on his second voyage.
chapters.lede: Every ocean is crossed, charted and contested within four centuries. The Atlantic's largest cargo by value and by consequence is enslaved people.
chapters.cite: Eltis & Richardson; Solar & de Zwart (2017); Portuguese *Regimento*.

chapters.title: Iron hulls and steam propulsion
chapters.text:
Between 1800 and 1900 a sea passage changed from something negotiated with the wind into something bought with coal, and the change was driven by fuel economy rather than by power. An early paddle steamer burned so much coal for its output that it had little room for cargo on a long route. John Elder's compound engine of 1854 used the steam twice, at two pressures; triple expansion, in general service from about 1881, used it three times. Coal consumption fell from roughly 4.5 lb per indicated horsepower-hour to about 1.5, and at that figure a steamer could carry enough fuel to cross an ocean and still earn freight.

Hull material changed with it. Iron allowed longer hulls than timber could span — Brunel's SS Great Britain of 1843 combined an iron hull with a screw propeller, and his Great Eastern of 1858 was 211 m long and six times the tonnage of anything afloat, a ship for which no trade existed until she was used to lay the transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and could not be used under sail: there is no working wind in the cut, and a sailing ship had to be towed. It shortened London to Bombay by around 4,500 nautical miles for steamers and by nothing at all for sail, which removed the eastern trades from sailing ships in a single stroke. Cutty Sark was launched that same year — the fastest sailing ships ever built were launched in the decade that made them commercially obsolete.

Britain held the resulting business: by 1900 British yards had built and British owners operated something close to a third of world tonnage, supported by coaling stations, cable routes and marine insurance concentrated in London. Germany and the United States were building competitive fleets by the end of the century, and Japan after the Meiji restoration constructed a modern navy largely in British yards before building its own.
chapters.lede: Within a single lifetime, passage times stop depending mainly on the wind and start depending on fuel and engine power.
chapters.cite: Griffiths, *Steam at Sea*; Suez Canal Authority.

chapters.title: Steel warships and two wars at sea
chapters.stat: Battle of the Atlantic: ~14.7 M tons sunk by U-boats
chapters.text:
HMS Dreadnought, commissioned in 1906, carried ten 12-inch guns on one hull and steam turbines that gave her 21 knots. An all-big-gun ship could be spotted and corrected at ranges where a mixed battery could not, and she was fast enough to choose the range; every battleship then afloat, including Britain's own, was devalued at a stroke, and the naval arms race that followed was one of the conditions of 1914. Oil firing and the diesel motorship — the Danish Selandia of 1912 was the first ocean-going example — followed within a decade.

Both world wars turned on merchant shipping rather than on fleet actions. Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917 and came close to succeeding; the countermeasure was convoy, resisted by the Admiralty on the argument that it presented a larger target, and adopted only under pressure. It worked, because a convoy is not a bigger target but a rarer one: the ocean is mostly empty, and a submarine has to find it first.

The Battle of the Atlantic was decided in May 1943, when the mid-ocean air gap south of Greenland was finally closed by very-long-range Liberators and escort carriers. Losses among the U-boat arm were the heaviest of any branch of the German military: of roughly 40,000 men who served in submarines, some 30,000 did not return. On the Allied side the answer was construction faster than sinking — 2,710 Liberty ships were built to one welded, prefabricated design, at an average of around 42 days each.

The shipbuilding centres of the period were Britain, Germany, the United States and Japan, and the war ended with American yards holding a capacity none of the others could match.
chapters.lede: In both wars the decisive question is whether merchant shipping can cross the Atlantic in sufficient quantity.
rows: adopted 1917 — a convoy is a rarer target, not a bigger one

chapters.title: Containerisation and modern shipping
chapters.stat: ~24,000 TEU in one hull; ~80% of world trade by volume
chapters.text:
On 26 April 1956 a converted tanker named Ideal-X sailed from Newark to Houston with 58 steel boxes on deck. The boxes themselves were not new; the standard was. Malcom McLean's contribution was insisting that the container be a single interchangeable unit that could move between ship, rail and lorry without being unpacked, and the ISO dimensions adopted between 1968 and 1970 made that true worldwide.

The cost that disappeared was handling. Break-bulk cargo was loaded piece by piece by large gangs of dockers, and a ship could spend as long in port as at sea. Containerisation cut that to hours and cut the labour with it, which is why the change was fought bitterly on the waterfront and why it moved ports out of the cities that had grown around them: New York's business went to Newark and Elizabeth, London's to Tilbury and then Felixstowe, because the new requirement was deep water, backing land and rail access rather than proximity to a market.

Ship size then grew against fixed infrastructure rather than against the sea. Panamax describes not a ship but the inside dimensions of a lock chamber completed in 1914, and for most of a century it constrained the world's fleet; the canal's larger locks opened in 2016. The Maersk Triple-E class of 2013 carried about 18,000 twenty-foot equivalent units, and the largest ships now approach 24,000.

Around 11 billion tonnes of cargo move by sea each year, on the order of 80 per cent of world merchandise trade by volume. The industry's centre moved with the manufacturing it serves: American and European yards gave way to Japan, then South Korea, then China, while ownership concentrated in a small number of operators and registration moved largely to open registries.
chapters.lede: A steel container of standard dimensions removes most of the cost of transferring cargo between ship, rail and road — and much of the reason a port is where it is.
chapters.cite: Levinson, *The Box* (2006); UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport.
